Minor Hotels to manage Gardens of Eden resort in Phuket, slated to open in 2031
article:
Thailand-based hospitality operator Minor Hotels has signed a hotel management agreement with Amal Group of Companies for Gardens of Eden Resort Phuket. This marks the first property under its Minor Reserve Collection luxury brand in Asia.

Scheduled to open in 2031, the resort will be located in Bang Tao, Phuket, comprising a 100-key hotel and 210 one- to three-bedroom residences. It will form the hospitality centrepiece of Gardens of Eden, a 33-acre integrated luxury living and wellness development by Amal Group that will also comprise Etro Residences and Gardens of Eden Residences.

The resort will feature a wellness facility spanning more than 53,820 sq ft. Guests will also have access to a range of dining options, including an all-day dining restaurant, two specialty restaurants, an organic café and a lobby lounge.

“Thailand is home for Minor Hotels, so introducing the new Gardens of Eden Phuket, Minor Reserve Collection to the kingdom is a significant milestone for our company and our luxury brand strategy,” said Omar Romero, chief development and luxury officer, Minor Hotels.

Alexander Chuvalov, CEO of Gardens of Eden, added: “Phuket remains one of the world's most attractive resort markets, and we believe the combination of Minor Hotels' luxury hospitality expertise and the strength of the Gardens of Eden vision will create a distinctive offering for both international travellers and residents.”

Gardens of Eden Resort Phuket will join a growing global portfolio of Minor Reserve Collection properties, which includes 640 hotels, resorts and branded residences across 67 countries.

title: DBS, Singtel or Microsoft: 3 Very Different Stocks for a Long-Term Portfolio
article:
The best stock for a
long-term portfolio
isn’t always the one with the best share price run.
So, what should you look for, and could one portfolio hold three very different companies?
DBS Group Holdings Ltd
(SGX: D05) is Singapore’s biggest bank.
Singapore Telecommunications Limited
(SGX: Z74), or Singtel, runs telcos here and in Australia, and owns stakes in phone companies around the region.
Microsoft Corporation
(NASDAQ: MSFT) is the US software giant behind Windows and the Azure cloud.
They do quite different jobs in a portfolio.
DBS and Singtel are mainly there for the dividends, while you’d own Microsoft for growth.
DBS: A Dividend-Paying Banking Powerhouse
Start with the one that is a favourite among Singapore investors.
DBS
has operations spread across Asia, and it is very good at making money.
In its latest results, for the first half of 2026 (1H2026), the bank earned a record net profit of S$6.01 billion.
Crucially, this was achieved with a stunning return on equity (ROE) of 17.9%, which is the best among the three local banks.
DBS’s wealth management business helped, with fees from affluent clients hitting a record S$1.83 billion.
That money flowed back to shareholders.
Over the last twelve months (LTM), DBS returned S$3.18 per share in dividends to shareholders (of which S$0.60 per share was a capital return, with the rest being ordinary dividends).
That works out to a trailing yield of 4.3%.
DBS can afford it.
Its capital cushion, the common equity tier 1 (CET1) ratio, is healthy at 14.6%. and only 1.0% of its loans have gone bad.
Falling interest rates are the main risk for DBS investors.
Banks earn less on the loans they disburse when rates decline.
DBS is not immune to this, although loan growth and fee income from areas such as wealth management can help cushion the impact.
Slower loan growth and rising credit costs could also weigh on the bank’s earnings.
The key takeaway is that DBS is a fine choice if you’re seeking dividends from an established bank, as long as you accept the interest-rate and economic risks that accompany it.
Singtel: A Combination of Dividends and Regional Growth
Singtel is a different animal.
People keep paying phone and internet bills whatever the economy does, and that steady stream is what the company is built on.
It runs telcos in Singapore and Australia (the latter through Optus).
Ownership stakes in telcos across the region, such as Airtel in India and AIS in Thailand, provide further geographical diversification.
For the financial year ended 31 March 2026 (FY2026), Singtel generated S$2.44 billion in free cash flow.
In the three months to 30 June 2026 (1QFY2027), Singtel’s regional stakes earned S$543 million in profit after tax, up 16% year on year (YoY).
Its data centre arm, Digital InfraCo, grew its top line by 19%, and Optus lifted its EBIT (earnings before interest and taxes) by 14%.
Consequently, Singtel’s underlying profit rose 21% from a year ago to S$831 million.
The dividend needs a careful read.
Singtel paid S$0.185 per share for FY2026, but only S$0.134 per share was a regular dividend.
The other S$0.051 came from selling assets, something that can’t go on forever.
Singtel still has about S$2.25 billion in planned asset disposals to complete, after which the additional payout might cease.
At current prices, this translates to a dividend yield of 4.5%.
The risks for the telco giant include intensifying competition for its telco operations and capital expenditure needed to grow its data centre business.
Currency swings are something to pay attention to as well.
On balance, Singtel gives you steady telco cash flow and a slice of the digitalisation and data centre boom.
However, as noted above, its extra dividend payout could be curtailed once its asset disposal programme runs its course.
Microsoft: A Global Technology Growth Engine
Microsoft is the odd one out.
It pays a dividend, but investors buy it for growth.
Much of its revenue recurs.
Businesses pay for Microsoft 365 through subscriptions, while Azure, its cloud platform, bills them for what they actually use.
Microsoft says what sets Azure apart is the hybrid cloud architecture, which lets companies run their own servers alongside it.
Artificial intelligence
(AI) has given Azure a real push.
In the first quarter of its FY2027 (1QFY2027), Azure revenue grew 48% YoY, while total revenue rose 19% YoY to US$92.3 billion.
The catch is how much Microsoft is spending to keep up.
It put US$115.9 billion into property and equipment in FY2026, and it hasn’t slowed down since.
Capital spending hit US$46 billion in 1QFY2027, which knocked free cash flow down to US$18.6 billion.
Shareholders weren’t left out, though.
Microsoft still handed back US$10.2 billion through dividends and buybacks in the quarter, and the hope is that all this spending shows up as bigger profits a few years from now.
You do pay for that growth.
Microsoft trades at about 27 times forward earnings.
The dividend was recently raised 8% to US$0.98 a quarter, but that still only works out to a yield of about 0.75%.
This valuation leaves little room for error, given strong competition from rival cloud providers and AI model makers.
Microsoft may appeal to investors prioritising long-term capital appreciation, although its relatively low dividend yield makes it less suitable for those seeking substantial immediate income.
Should You Own All Three in One Portfolio?
You could, and the mix makes sense.
Banks, telcos and tech companies tend to behave differently.
DBS and Singtel provide reliable dividend income (reinvesting payments received can further turbocharge your compounding journey), while Microsoft provides a stronger growth angle for the portfolio.
But three stocks alone aren’t a portfolio.
Both DBS and Singtel depend heavily on the region, so if the region slows down, you’d feel it in both at once.
Microsoft brings a different problem: it earns in US dollars, leaving you exposed to currency swings.
It’s better to see these three as a starting point, not your whole portfolio.
Get Smart: Different Stocks, Different Roles
So which stock should you pick?
That is the wrong question.
Instead, ask what your portfolio is missing.
If you need income, DBS and Singtel do the heavy lifting.
If you want growth, Microsoft is the one.
Each does a different job, and a good portfolio needs more than one of them.

title: Chinese stock sell-off resumes as rescue tools face scepticism
article:
(Nov 3): China’s efforts to stem a market rout by reviving tools from the 2024 downturn were met with scepticism as stocks resumed their sell-off.

The two liquidity-injection tools — a swap facility and relending operations to encourage more stock purchases — reappeared with some adjustments as authorities sought to bolster market stability. Turnover in exchange-traded funds favoured by the national team also surged to 120 billion yuan (US$18 billion or $23 billion), the highest since late January, suggesting state investors actively stepped in.

Markets weren’t impressed. The tech-heavy Star 50 Index tumbled nearly 4% on Tuesday, erasing gains from the previous session when anticipation of policy support drove markets higher. The CSI 300 Index, an onshore benchmark, slipped as much as 1.2% before closing 0.2% lower.

The slide shows re-utilising 2024 tools has lacked the shock-and-awe effect needed to reignite animal spirits. The pivot back then stunned investors on multiple fronts, combining the new equity-support facilities with rate cuts to signal strong determination to reviving stocks. Yet a crisis of confidence has become more entrenched now with sluggish economic growth and uncertainty over earnings, suggesting a more structural policy reset is needed.

“The measures are likely to have only a limited marginal impact, as these tools have been available for the past two years and are not new sources of incremental support,” said Fu Zhifeng, the chief investment officer of Shanghai Chengzhou Investment Management. “The meeting is more significant as a policy signal, showing regulators’ intention to stabilise the market.”

Chinese shares have been mired in a slump since the summer amid a weak economy and doubts over artificial intelligence (AI) earnings. The CSI 300 Index fell 8.5% in October, its worst monthly decline in more than a decade, and dropped for a record 12 straight weeks through last Friday.

In a Monday statement, the People’s Bank of China (PBOC) said it will conduct operations under its securities, funds and insurance companies swap facility when appropriate, allowing them to exchange assets for more liquid ones to fund stock purchases. It will also increase the number of participating institutions and moderately lower swap fees.

Separately, the PBOC will cut the rate on its relending facility to 1% from 1.25%, make the programme permanent, and encourage banks to increase lending. The facility provides low-cost central bank funding to banks for loans that finance companies’ share buy-backs and stake increases by major shareholders.

See also: China vows to boost yuan liquidity, back Hong Kong markets

The swap operations will begin in the coming days, with 31 securities and fund firms approved to participate and applying for more than 100 billion yuan of quotas, the China Securities Regulatory Commission (CSRC) said in a statement. The relending programme will be broadened, including by encouraging more major index constituents and leading technology companies to participate, it said.

The CSRC also plans to ease buy-back rules, facilitating repurchases when shares fall below the IPO price and requiring companies with excess fundraising proceeds to buy back shares when market-support conditions are triggered. It will also study changes to margin-financing requirements as a countercyclical measure to mobilise existing funds and improve market liquidity, suggesting scope to ease leverage restrictions.

About 440 billion yuan of loans supporting share buy-backs and stake increases have been contracted, with more than 280 billion yuan disbursed, according to the central bank. The outstanding balance of the swap facility is 105 billion yuan.

The regulators have also told banks to hold fire on company listings and large share sales, another attempt to put a floor under the rout, the Financial Times reported on Tuesday.

The Monday meeting was attended by 23 securities firms, funds and 26 banks. Representatives of China International Capital Corp, Guotai Haitong Securities Co, Citic Securities Co, Industrial & Commercial Bank of China Ltd, China Construction Bank Corp and China Citic Bank Corp were among those who spoke, the PBOC said.

“Overall I think it’s an effort to stabilise its financial markets, but it has a clear long-term perspective rather than an immediate reward,” said Anna Wu, an investment strategist and founder of Floodlines Research. “A real turnaround needs demand-side fiscal support that reaches households, a steadier property market, and evidence that earnings, especially in AI and tech, can justify valuations.”

title: Swiss inflation accelerates to highest in almost three years
article:
(Nov 3): Switzerland’s inflation rate rose to the highest level in almost three years, driven by the surge in oil costs and a weaker franc.

Consumer prices increased 1.5% from a year earlier in October, the statistics office said on Tuesday (Nov 3). That’s up from 1% in September and stronger than predicted by any of the economists in a Bloomberg survey.

While the reading is within the Swiss National Bank’s 0-2% range, it is already noticeably above the 1.2% forecast of policymakers for the fourth quarter. Officials see most of the acceleration as temporary and have said that medium-term pressures increased only slightly.

SNB borrowing costs have been at the world’s lowest level of zero for more than a year, in part because the cost shock from the Iran war has been benign in Switzerland. Petrol prices have risen but a smaller share of energy in the Swiss inflation basket has kept that from driving the gauge.

In October, rising prices for heating oil, petrol and diesel drove inflation, the statistics office said. So-called core inflation, which excludes volatile elements such as energy, held steady at 0.5%.

The acceleration in Switzerland remains muted compared to the surrounding euro area, where the fallout from the Iran war probably drove price growth to twice the European Central Bank’s target last month. According to the harmonised European methodology, Swiss inflation in October was 1.6%, versus an expected 4% in the currency bloc.

Over the past months, a continued weakening of the franc has boosted domestic cost increases, as buying abroad became pricier for the Swiss. Policymakers acknowledged this at their most recent rate decision in September, dialling down their threat of intervention after some action to weaken the currency.

title: Bayer raises profit outlook on strong demand for drugs
article:
(Nov 3): Bayer AG raised its annual profit outlook after increased demand for some of its newer drugs drove a better-than-expected performance at its pharmaceutical unit.

Adjusted earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation are now expected between €9.8 billion and €10.3 billion this year, the German company said Tuesday, slightly above its previous forecast range.

Sales of prostate cancer drug Nubeqa and kidney therapy Kerendia exceeded expectations in the quarter, prompting CEO Bill Anderson to say in a statement that Bayer has “reached a turning point in pharma’s growth trajectory".

Third-quarter earnings of €1.62 billion also exceeded the average estimate of analysts surveyed by Bloomberg.

The boost comes as the German conglomerate is focused on containing its biggest problem: mass litigation in the US over claims that its Roundup weedkiller causes cancer, which the company denies. Bayer inherited the litigation with its 2018 acquisition of Monsanto and has already paid more than US$11 billion to resolve Roundup claims.

Bayer’s shares are up about 35% this year on optimism the company may be finally getting to grips with the issue.

See also: Danone sales rise on higher prices, medical nutrition demand

Anderson has pledged to “significantly” contain the legal overhang by the end of this year through a multi-pronged strategy, including a settlement. Bayer already won a favourable US Supreme Court ruling in June and is now awaiting a final nod on its US$7.25 billion settlement proposal, which is designed to resolve most current and future claims.

In the third quarter, the pharmaceutical division posted sales and profit growth, with Nubeqa hitting about €1 billion in the period. That helped offset generic competition for blood thinner Xarelto, whose sales slumped by 30%, as well as eye medicine Eylea. The company recently received its first approval for its potential blockbuster stroke drug, Asundexian, in China.

Bayer raised its full-year adjusted earnings margin target for the unit to as much as 27%, from a previous peak of 25%.

See also: What to know about plague after suspected Russia lab worker case

Meanwhile, earnings at the crop science division fell 41% in the quarter, in part driven by higher costs and weaker crop-protection sales. Earlier this year, Bayer separated the US glyphosate business into an entity called Ruveon, a move seen as an attempt to limit litigation risks.

Consumer health, the smallest unit, posted broadly flat sales. The division continued to face headwinds from weakness in the US.

title: Türkiye inflation quickens unexpectedly, clouding rate path
article:
(Nov 3): Turkish inflation accelerated slightly in October, raising questions about the possibility of another interest-rate cut before the end of the year.

Annual consumer price growth picked up to 29.8% from 29.7% in September, TurkStat said on Tuesday. The median estimate in a Bloomberg survey of 22 analysts was 29.5%.

Monthly price growth was 2.58%, quickening from 1.84% the previous month and coming in above the median analyst forecast of 2.40%. Clothing, shoe, food and non-alcoholic-beverage prices were among the biggest contributors to the monthly rise.

The central bank cut its benchmark interest rate by 100 basis points to 36% in October, its first reduction since January, citing subdued demand and slowing economic activity. The latest inflation print may complicate economists’ forecast of another 100-basis-point cut during the year’s final rate-setting meeting on Dec 10, though the central bank will be able to assess November inflation ahead of the decision.

Turkish stocks and bonds fell following the inflation data. The yield on two-year and 10-year bonds rose by eight basis points and six basis points, respectively. The Borsa Istanbul 100 Index fell as much as 1%, led by a decline in bank stocks.

The lira was little changed, trading at close to 50 per US dollar.

See also: Disney plans thousands of layoffs, targeting 20% cost savings — Bloomberg

Policymakers last month said they expected headline inflation to keep slowing despite a pickup in the seasonally adjusted cost of services. Governor Fatih Karahan will present the central bank’s latest projections in Istanbul on Nov 12.

Inflation risks “are heavily tilted to the upside", Bloomberg Economics’ Selva Bahar Baziki wrote in advance of the data. “A sustained escalation in the Middle East could derail the expected decline in inflation.”

“Renewed Middle East conflict could also exacerbate the currency weakness triggered by the recent fund rout, adding to price pressures,” she added.

title: US moves to revoke South Africa, Rwanda duty-free trade access
article:
(Nov 3): The US announced plans to revoke South Africa and Rwanda’s access to a duty-free trade pact, intensifying pressure on two African nations whose relations with Washington have become increasingly fraught.

The two countries will no longer qualify for benefits under the African Growth and Opportunity Act after US President Donald Trump found their governments “are engaging in practices that are inconsistent with AGOA’s eligibility criteria”, US Trade Representative Ambassador Jamieson Greer said in a statement on Monday.

“These concerning and pervasive practices include, but are not limited to, barriers that undermine American trade and investment that pose a threat to US national security,” Greer said.

South Africa’s government has been bracing for bad news on its continued eligibility as ties between Washington and Pretoria have deteriorated since Trump returned to the White House last year. Relations between Rwanda and the US have been strained by Kigali’s involvement in the conflict in the neighbouring Democratic Republic of Congo.

AGOA grants tariff-free access to the world’s largest economy for more than 1,800 products and has helped to boost trade between the US and the region since its inception in 2000. South Africa — the largest beneficiary of AGOA — exported US$1.63 billion of goods to America last year under the pact, while Rwanda shipped US$1.48 million, according to US International Trade Commission data.

“Government is working closely with affected industries to assess the implications and will continue to provide appropriate support on a company-to-company basis,” South Africa’s trade minister, Parks Tau, said in a statement. “AGOA remains important to South Africa, but it does not constitute the totality of the economic relationship between South Africa and the United States.”

See also: How’s the US-China tech war going? Ask AI

After returning to power, Trump quickly froze US assistance to South Africa, falsely claiming the government is allowing a genocide of White Afrikaner farmers. Trump has also criticised the country’s Black economic-empowerment laws, which were introduced to address inequalities created by apartheid.

America ranks as South Africa’s third-biggest trading partner, after China and the European Union. Bilateral trade between South Africa and the US last year was US$24.1 billion — less than half the US$55.6 billion of commerce with China, according to data compiled by Bloomberg.

Pretoria has been trying to agree to a broader trade deal with Washington after Trump unveiled harsh tariffs that penalise its automobile sector, potentially putting jobs at risk in a country with one of the highest levels of unemployment in the world.

See also: Singapore’s top envoy on mission to soothe Indonesian angst

South Africa’s main exports to the US under AGOA include agricultural products, including citrus fruits and auto parts.

“This will be a loss not just for us, but the US consumer will lose too,” the Citrus Growers’ Association of Southern Africa said in a statement following the news. “Seasonal fresh produce does not threaten US jobs. It helps keep America healthy and also helps contain food inflation,” said CGA CEO Boitshoko Ntshabele.

The Trump administration’s concerns about Rwanda include barriers to trade and investment, the rule of law and political pluralism, according to the statement. In South Africa, it said, the administration is deeply concerned about barriers to US trade and investment, corruption and threats to US national security and foreign-policy interests.

“It’s yet another trade decision grounded in grievance that flies in the face of what responsible policy should be,” Representative Richard Neal of Massachusetts, the ranking Democrat on the US House Ways and Means Committee, said in a statement. “The power of our trade laws shouldn’t be twisted so Trump can further policies based on biased accusations made by those in his orbit looking to settle scores.”

title: IEA issues warning on gas market tightness extending into 2027
article:
(Nov 3): Tightness in the world’s natural gas market could extend well into next year as Europe risks ending this winter with record-low fuel inventories and will need to replenish them, according to the International Energy Agency.

Low gas storage levels across the European Union, coupled with continued supply disruptions in the Middle East, mean that the region will drain its reserves heavily over the cold months, the IEA said in a report Tuesday (Nov 3).

“EU storage sites could close the 2026/27 heating season with record low inventories,” it said. That would “substantially increase the need for injections through summer 2027, potentially extending market tightness into the following year”.

Europe’s economies have struggled with gas prices near their highest levels since the energy crisis erupted four years ago. Even though the continent is just starting its peak-demand winter season, next year’s risks are already spreading into 2027 futures contracts as traders hedge against further price increases.

Europe’s next May contracts have been trading above those for November 2027 as the market weighs risks to supply, including continued hostilities in the Middle East and potential delays to new gas projects. The spread reached a record high in recent days.

IEA’s simulations show that EU gas storage levels could drop below 10% of working capacity — a record low — by the end of March, “assuming a worst case” of continued disruption to LNG flows via the crucial Strait of Hormuz and colder weather. This would leave the European market exposed to late cold spells, the IEA said, meaning even more price volatility by the end of the heating season.

See also: BP gets US$6 bil to pay down debt as Castrol deal closes

The Paris-based agency expects the market to remain tight even though new LNG capacities are coming online next year and global demand for the fuel is expected to drop in 2026, including by 3% in Europe. The continent’s factories are forecast to cut gas consumption by 5% given elevated price levels — in addition to the continued expansion of renewables across Europe.

The IEA report estimates that trade flows through the Strait of Hormuz will remain largely disrupted, at least until the end of the year. Under this assumption, global LNG supply is projected to decline by 3% this year, the steepest annual decline on record.

title: Central banks buy gold at fastest pace since 2024, WGC says
article:
(Nov 3): Central banks bought gold at the fastest pace since the end of 2024 in the third quarter, even as the metal faced pressure from higher oil prices and interest rates.

The institutions accumulated a net of 321 tonnes in the three months through September, the World Gold Council said in a report on Tuesday (Nov 3). After a slow start to 2026, that brought the estimate for year-to-date buying to 675 tonnes, slightly ahead of the same period a year earlier.

The figures underscore how central banks — an important driver of bullion’s multiyear rally to a record high in January — have remained a key support to prices in an otherwise tepid market. The metal has lost about a quarter of its value since the Iran war began in late February, as higher energy costs fuelled expectations of tighter monetary policy, a headwind for the non-yielding metal.

Weaker gold prices during the quarter likely encouraged some central banks to step up purchases, said John Reade, senior market strategist at the WGC. For central banks with a bearish outlook on the US dollar, the greenback’s rally may also have made shifting some reserves into gold more appealing, he said.

“If you think the dollar is going to be falling in the long term, and you own short-dated Treasuries and they’re rolling off, then maybe you’re taking some of those expensive dollars and buying gold with them,” Reade said.

See also: Gold climbs back from one-year low as dip buyers arrest slide

Almost two-thirds of the estimated central-bank buying wasn’t disclosed by monetary authorities themselves. Consultancy Metals Focus Ltd. calculates purchases on behalf of the council using a combination of public data, trade statistics and field research.

China and Poland were the biggest disclosed buyers in the latest quarter, adding 63 tonnes and 41 tonnes, respectively. Russia was the only major seller, offloading 19 tonnes in the period.

Gold has drifted lower in recent months, as war in the Middle East continues to push crude prices and interest-rate expectations higher. Still, inflows into gold-backed exchange-traded funds have been markedly strong, with holdings rising by 211 tonnes to a record in the third quarter, the WGC said.

Jewellery demand fell 17% to 313 tonnes, the weakest third quarter in the council’s data going back to 2000, as tax changes in India and China, along with higher prices, pushed consumers toward lighter and lower-carat pieces.

Also in the WGC report:
• Recycling fell 8% to 314 tonnes, the lowest since 2023.
• Bar and coin demand fell 19% to 268 tonnes. However, those purchases rose 7% to 79 tonnes in China, lifting year-to-date buying there to a record 393 tonnes.

title: Grab raises sales, earnings forecasts on rising ride demand
article:
(Nov 3): Grab Holdings Ltd raised its full-year revenue and profit forecasts after quarterly earnings beat estimates, signalling confidence that rising ride-hailing and food-delivery demand across Southeast Asia will offset regulatory hurdles.

Sales will rise as high as US$4.2 billion ($5.4 billion) this year, while adjusted earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortisation (Ebitda) will expand to as much as US$800 million, the company said on Tuesday. In August, it had forecast sales of as much as US$4.15 billion and earnings on that basis of up to US$740 million.

The stock rose more than 6% in after-hours trading, with the forecast suggesting Grab is fending off competition from the likes of Indonesia’s GoTo Group. Grab added about three million monthly users in the quarter through September for a total of 57 million as more consumers in Southeast Asia go online.

Meanwhile, higher fuel prices are raising ride and delivery costs across the region of about 700 million people. Platform companies are offering incentives to drivers and customers to soften the blow, but that risks squeezing already thin margins.

Competition remains intense, with GoTo and new entrants like Green & Smart Mobility JSC vying against Grab in populous markets like Indonesia and Vietnam. Uber Technologies Inc, one of Grab’s backers, could also be a looming threat — its planned acquisition of Delivery Hero SE opens up a path for Uber Eats to re-enter Southeast Asia. Alphabet Inc’s Waymo also plans to launch robotaxis in Singapore in 2028.

See also: State Street CEO says it’s ‘hard to see’ AI as a bubble yet

Shares of Grab had dropped more than 40% this year through Monday’s regular trading, cutting its market value to US$11.7 billion.

Regulators are also piling on pressure. Indonesia, one of Grab’s biggest markets, has already cut the maximum commission companies can charge on scooter rides, and is considering further rules in areas like food delivery by the end of the year. Grab is in talks with the Indonesian government about potential delivery commission cap changes, chief financial officer Peter Oey said in an interview.

The company is also striking deals to spur growth beyond its core business. In September, it agreed to acquire a majority stake in buy-now-pay-later platform Atome Financial for US$1.49 billion, after buying US-based Stash Financial for an enterprise value of US$425 million. But not every deal has gone to plan. Last month, Taiwan’s Fair Trade Commission blocked Grab’s roughly US$600 million purchase of Foodpanda’s local delivery operations on antitrust concerns.

See also: Adani Group said to seek US$1.5 bil for data centre financing — Bloomberg

“We’re very disappointed about Taiwan,” Oey said. “From a geography expansion perspective, we will look at other opportunities, but we are very focused also on Southeast Asia.”

In the latest quarter, adjusted Ebitda rose 74% to US$237 million, the Singapore-based company said. Analysts projected US$194.2 million on average, according to Bloomberg-compiled data. Revenue grew 27% to US$1.1 billion, roughly in line with estimates.

To add users, Grab has expanded its product offering to include more affordable and premium options. It’s also expanding into games and microdramas, partnering with other platforms to keep users on its app for longer.

title: Onshore yuan snaps winning streak as PBOC lifts FX reserve ratio
article:
(Nov 3): The onshore yuan ended its longest winning streak in three decades after the People’s Bank of China moved to cool its rally by asking banks to hold more foreign currencies in reserve.

The yuan weakened as much as 0.4% to 6.6731 per dollar onshore, halting 13 straight days of gains, which was the longest streak since 1996, according to data compiled by Bloomberg. It also dropped as much as 0.4% in offshore trading. The PBOC’s move forces banks to lock up more foreign exchange, reducing the supply of dollars and easing the appreciation pressure on the yuan.

The move is “aimed at moderating the pace of yuan appreciation rather than reversing its direction”, said Cindy Keung, economist at OCBC Bank (Hong Kong). “While the official objective is to strengthen foreign exchange liquidity management, the move also sends a clear policy signal that authorities are seeking to prevent excessive and rapid yuan appreciation.”

The yuan has advanced over 4% against the greenback this year to outperform most of its Asian peers, thanks to surging exports, heavy corporate conversion flows and the central bank’s tolerance for a stronger currency. That resilience has held up even as mounting expectations of Federal Reserve interest-rate hikes bolstered the dollar.

The central bank will increase the ratio by two percentage points from the current 4% to 6%, according to a statement. The move takes effect on Nov 15. The PBOC last raised the ratio in December 2021, when it asked financial institutions to hold 9% of their foreign exchange in reserve. It was the second increase that year, after the central bank raised the ratio by two percentage points in June.

See also: Weaker euro boosts European exporters as earnings season peaks

“The move will withdraw about US$24 billion from the market,” said Zhaopeng Xing, senior China strategist at Australia & New Zealand Banking Group, referring to the latest reduction. “It is relatively low comparing with net FX sales monthly US$30 billion this year. The move is symbolic. More measures will be possible if market imbalance remains in place.”

The PBOC also set its daily reference rate more than 600 pips weaker than estimates on Tuesday, the largest bias since early September. The so-called fixing limits the onshore yuan’s movements to 2% on either side of the reference rate, signalling official pushback against rapid appreciation.

The latest central bank measures also come amid expectations that the currency would benefit from seasonal tailwinds. Exporters typically step up yuan purchases around year-end to meet accounting and pre-Lunar New Year funding needs, contributing to the currency’s seasonal strength. As cross-border e-commerce becomes a larger source of China’s trade surplus, global holiday shopping may be turning into a more meaningful driver of yuan demand.

See also: Marcos pledges to ‘do all we can’ to defend Philippine peso

“It is ahead of the FX sales season in 4Q. The tightening will help rebalance the flows and slow the appreciation pace of the yuan,” said ANZ’s Xing.

For Fiona Lim, a senior FX strategist at Malayan Banking Berhad, the timing of the PBOC’s move is likely linked to global political events.

“Given that it happens just before the US midterm elections, this could be to prevent yuan appreciation from gathering pace in an environment of lower oil [and a] Democrat sweep that could be negative for the dollar,” she said.

title: Huafa’s US$62 bil debt strain shakes China’s credit market
article:
(Nov 3): China’s credit market just suffered its worst selloff in two years as a major conglomerate’s plunge into distress tests the assumption that government ties can protect state-owned firms from financial peril.

In just a few days, Zhuhai Huafa Group Co called that view into question. The conglomerate, wholly-owned by local governments in the southern province of Guangdong, missed payments on two trust products and asked to extend some bank loans, people familiar with the matter said last Monday.

By Friday, unease was mounting as investors came to terms with the implications in a country where missed debt payments by state-owned firms had become rare. Over the two days through Monday, money managers pushed the average yield they demand to hold benchmark Chinese corporate bonds up 10.3 basis points, the worst two-day stretch since October 2024. Those rates on three-year yuan notes with the same local AAA ratings as Huafa were little changed Tuesday (Nov 3) morning, traders said.

The crisis at Huafa, which has helped build landmarks such as the 330m tall Zhuhai Tower skyscraper, is spotlighting risks among Chinese state-owned firms reliant on implicit government support as a years-long property downturn and slowing economic growth hurt profitability. Its offshore bonds tumbled to distressed levels as low as about 54% of face value last week, as concern mounted over its RMB413 billion of interest-bearing liabilities.

“Local government financing vehicles and some state-owned firms with weak standalone credit profiles are just a ticking time bomb,” said Zerlina Zeng, head of Asia credit strategy at Creditsights Singapore.

See also: China vows to boost yuan liquidity, back Hong Kong markets

The shock from Huafa even briefly spilled beyond the onshore credit market. Chinese high-yield dollar notes suffered their worst week in about a year last week. In the local sovereign debt market, 30-year government bond futures posted their biggest daily drop since March on Friday, with traders citing Huafa as a drag on sentiment across markets.

The conglomerate’s stumble stands out, after accommodative monetary policy in recent years and an unprecedented government push to contain debt risks tied to local authorities helped avoid such outcomes. It also raises concerns given Huafa’s home base of Guangdong, which has China’s biggest provincial economy.

“Almost every major financial institution I know holds Huafa bonds, especially state-owned institutions,” according to Li Huan, co-founder of asset manager Forest Capital Hong Kong Ltd.

See also: China to expand stock support tools to stabilise market

To some investors, the situation recalls refinancing stress that swept through China’s coal sector after a surprise default by a state-run miner roiled markets in late 2020. The miner ultimately made full payment on its bonds months later as local authorities moved to restore market confidence.

Huafa’s offshore yuan-denominated securities due in 2027 have pared some of their earlier losses, recovering to about 63% of face value. That comes after news that it had repaid one of its trust products and that its property arm made good on payments due Monday on a yuan note.

Still, uncertainty persists over the company’s liabilities in the longer term and, more broadly, over the extent to which China will support its debt-laden state-owned firms.

If Huafa continues to repay its public bonds and makes progress on asset monetisation, the concerns could prove to be a temporary liquidity crunch contained by local authorities, according to a research note from China Zheshang Bank Co. But bond extensions or even potential restructurings could trigger a broader reassessment of the state-owned sector, the note said.

Huafa is about 93.5% owned by Zhuhai’s State-Owned Assets Supervision and Administration Commission, with Guangdong’s provincial finance department owning the remainder. The company had about RMB765 billion in total assets as of March.

The conglomerate, which derived about half of its revenue from property development and urban operations last year while also running businesses spanning financial services and technology, had blamed the property downturn as the main reason for its profitability swings.

A few days ago, its real estate arm reported a RMB6.44 billion net loss in the first nine months of this year.

Huafa was placed last week on rating watch negative by Fitch Ratings, which scores it at BBB, toward the lower end of investment grade. The step signals the increased possibility of a downgrade.

Fitch cited the company’s “weakening debt-service coverage, approaching near-term debt maturities and widening issuer bond spreads amidst unconfirmed market rumours of potential debt-maturity extensions”.

title: Copper, tin fall with base metals on renewed AI stocks selloff
article:
(Nov 3): Copper and tin fell with other industrial metals, as a renewed selloff in technology stocks in Asia weakened the demand outlook for materials used in data centers and to solder circuit boards.

Both contracts dropped more than 1% on the London Metal Exchange as concerns persisted over spending and stretched valuations at artificial intelligence companies. Tin has plunged 10% this quarter, the worst performer among the LME’s six major metals.

Copper had risen on Monday, helped in part by a pullback in oil prices that could mitigate inflation pressures. The US and Iran have signalled a willingness to pursue peace talks, easing anxiety over the war’s impact on interest rates and global growth.

Still, macro conditions are putting a lot of pressure on metals, particularly given the possibility that the conflict could resume after the US midterm elections, said Xu Wanqiu, an analyst with Cofco Futures Co.

Copper fell 1.2% to US$14,180 a tonne as of 10.50am in Shanghai while tin declined 2.2% to US$48,550 a tonne. Aluminium dropped 1.1% to US$3,060.50 a tonne.

title: Singaporean plan to import clean power hits Indonesian hurdle
article:
(Nov 3): Indonesia will prioritise domestic energy needs over exporting electricity, according to a government minister, complicating a plan for the country to supply renewable power to Singapore.

“Indonesia will not be able to export electricity in the near future,” Energy and Mineral Resources Minister Bahlil Lahadalia said on Monday. “We still need electricity ourselves.” The minister appeared to soften his tone in subsequent remarks to local media, in which he said that exports would be possible only if prices met Indonesia’s requirements.

The comments cloud the outlook for a plan for Singapore to import clean energy from Indonesia via a subsea power cable. The city-state, which relies on imported natural gas for most of its electricity, has also approved other deals to bring in renewable power from Australia, Malaysia, Vietnam and Cambodia. The agreements are necessary if Singapore is to meet its goal of reaching net zero emissions by 2050.

Indonesia’s focus on its own power needs may also jeopardise the development of a Southeast Asian grid, an ambitious plan to connect the electricity networks of a region with around 700 million people.

Relations between Singapore and Indonesia have run into turbulence in recent months over haze from fires in the archipelago that has spread to neighbouring countries and a decision by Jakarta to reduce gas exports to the city-state.

See also: Singapore to strike ‘right balance’ between affordability and decarbonisation as it pursues energy security

title: China vows to boost yuan liquidity, back Hong Kong markets
article:
(Nov 3): China Vice Premier He Lifeng said China will continue to support a free and open economic environment in Hong Kong and boost offshore yuan liquidity in the financial hub.

He said in a video speech to the Global Financial Leaders’ Investment Summit in Hong Kong that building the city “remains a key strategy for China”, pledging full support for its long-term development and stability.

He also vowed to scale up yuan bond issuance in Hong Kong and support listings there. He said mainland financial institutions’ ability to withstand risks keeps improving, and that China’s economic momentum is shifting to new drivers.

The pledges come as Hong Kong works to reinforce its position as a global financial centre, with Beijing’s backing seen as central to attracting international capital and deepening the city’s offshore yuan market.

Li Hongyan, the deputy administrator of the State Administration of Foreign Exchange, pledged to consolidate the city’s financial development, cement its international financial centre status and its role as an offshore yuan hub.

Chinese regulators also said they would continue to expand cross border links between the mainland and the city.

See also: China to expand stock support tools to stabilise market

Li Chao, a vice-chairman of the China Securities Regulatory Commission, said this will include a yuan stock trading counter into the stock trading link while China will continue to open up as well as strengthen cross-border regulatory cooperation.

At the same time, Li said they will crack down on fraud in cross-border capital and illegal business operations.

title: Thailand set to approve higher EV import tax
article:
(Nov 3): Thailand approved a higher excise tax on some fully imported electric vehicles, stepping up efforts to protect its auto-manufacturing base and encourage automakers to produce locally.

Thailand's Excise Department Director-General Pornchai Thiraveja confirmed the cabinet’s approval on Tuesday (Nov 3) but declined to provide the final rate. Bloomberg News earlier reported that the government was considering raising the tax to around 30%.

The Thai Finance Ministry had proposed raising the tax on completely built-up electric vehicles that do not have local content from the current 10%. Thai media on Tuesday reported that officials were considering a rate of around 30%-40%.

The measure could reshape competition in one of Southeast Asia’s most important auto markets. Thailand has spent decades building the region’s biggest vehicle-manufacturing hub and more recently used subsidies and tax incentives to attract EV investment, much of it from Chinese automakers while its traditional manufacturing base remains dominated by Japanese brands.

The higher tax is designed to narrow the cost disadvantage for companies already producing vehicles in Thailand and encourage other EV makers to manufacture locally rather than supply the fast-growing market through imports.

The move comes as Thailand’s electric passenger-car imports more than doubled from a year earlier in September, with China supplying almost all of them.

See also: Thailand could tax EV imports around 30%, finance chief says

Finance Minister Ekniti Nitithanprapas plans to discuss the government’s new EV tax policy with Japanese investors, Krungthep Turakij reported earlier, during a Board of Investment roadshow in Japan in mid-November.

title: Pimco CEO warns AI financing on path to become ‘too much’
article:
(Nov 3): Artificial intelligence (AI)-related financing could grow to about US$10 trillion ($12.8 trillion) over the next five years, eventually reaching excessive levels, said Emmanuel Roman, the chief executive officer of Pacific Investment Management Co (Pimco).

Roman estimated that about US$2 trillion of financing needs could be created annually over the next five years to fund capital spending by the AI industry, compared with a US bond market of about US$12 trillion.

The amount is eventually “going to be too much”, Roman said during a panel with Blackstone Inc president Jon Gray at the 2026 Global Financial Leaders’ Investment Summit in Hong Kong on Tuesday.

“At some point in time, there’s going to be a downturn, and then things are going to break,” Roman said. He added that a downturn could be triggered by anything from rising US interest rates or war in the Middle East to a eurozone crisis.

Asked whether being too cautious or taking on too much risk would be the bigger mistake for portfolio construction today, Roman said the greater danger is taking on too much risk.

Gray struck a more bullish tone, saying “some of this scepticism today is probably healthy”, while adding that the broader AI trend points to more investment and substantially greater demand for capital.

See also: Goldman restricts traders and bankers from using some AI tools — Bloomberg

“What is happening is very powerful, and I think underestimating the productivity gains that are coming and the change in consumer and businesses, that’s a mistake,” Gray said.

title: State Street CEO says it’s ‘hard to see’ AI as a bubble yet
article:
(Nov 3): State Street Corp chairman and chief executive officer Ron O’Hanley said it’s “hard to see” AI as being a bubble yet, with demand supporting the massive investments being poured into the technology.

“It’s not like these data centres are being built on spec. I mean, there’s real orders behind them, and in most cases, there’s real companies behind them,” O’Hanley told Bloomberg Television’s David Ingles and Yvonne Man in an interview on Tuesday. “So right now, it’s hard to see that’s a bubble.”

“The question will be whether does AI become more efficient, such that all the capacity that’s being built we don’t need now,” he said on the sidelines of the Hong Kong Monetary Authority’s Global Financial Leaders’ Investment Summit.

The global AI race has fuelled a borrowing binge that has flooded markets with more than US$650 billion of debt in less than two years, according to data compiled by Bloomberg. That has raised concerns among investors as the spree pushes up bond yields and increases scrutiny of what many see as lofty valuations of AI-linked companies.

US stocks just saw a punishing week for tech shares as concerns over the cost and financing of the AI investment boom intensified after Alphabet Inc.’s earnings.

“A bit of a market selloff was probably overdue,” said O’Hanley. “It certainly doesn’t seem disorderly at this point.”

See also: Adani Group said to seek US$1.5 bil for data centre financing — Bloomberg

The State Street chief also said he’s been seeing a healthy amount of activity in Hong Kong’s hedge fund industry as global funds set up offices. But he stopped short of providing a guidance of the company’s expansion plans in the region, but adds that the city has continued to grow in importance in the global payments system.

“So we would anticipate seeing growth here” particularly around the digital and market activities, he said.
